rationale: While spasticity and spastic paraparesis are consistent hallmark features of the SPG93/NFU1-related spastic paraplegia phenotype, the hypothesis's assertion that it 'typically present[s] in late childhood to early adulthood' is contradicted by clinical reports and cohort characterizations. In Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022) and OMIM #620938, SPG93 is defined as an early-onset disorder with patients presenting as early as 4.5 months to early childhood (e.g., 27 months in Uzunhan et al., 2020). Furthermore, the hypothesis's denominator estimation ('4/4 to 8/8 across initial family descriptions') underestimates the expanded clinical cohorts describing 19 patients across 10 families manifesting a broad continuum from early-onset pure to complex spastic paraplegia, often with relapsing-remitting courses and leukoencephalopathy.

evidence.text: OMIM entry 620938 describes autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-93 (SPG93) as characterized by an early-onset pure to complex hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotype, noting a cohort of 19 patients aged 4.5 months to 25 years from 10 families reported by Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022).

conflicts: Age of onset: The hypothesis posits typical presentation in late childhood to early adulthood, whereas OMIM #620938, Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022), and Uzunhan et al. (2020) emphasize an early-onset phenotype (infancy to early childhood, spanning from 4.5 months to early toddlerhood).

Clinical trajectory and course: Several sources report a relapsing-remitting course rather than a purely insidious, continuous progressive spasticity, frequently accompanied by cavitating leukoencephalopathy, hyperglycinemia, and peripheral neuropathy.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic breakdown of age of onset across all 19 patients described in Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the exact median and interquartile range of onset age will resolve whether infantile/early childhood onset predominates over late-childhood/adulthood onset.

new_directions.question_text: To what degree do elevated glycine levels and cavitating white matter lesions on MRI discriminate NFU1/SPG93 from classical hereditary spastic paraplegias (e.g., SPG4, SPG7, SPG11)?
new_directions.rationale: Identifying pathognomonic biochemical (hyperglycinemia) and neuroimaging (cavitating leukodystrophy) hallmarks would allow clinicians to accurately differentiate SPG93 from phenotypically overlapping spastic paraplegias.
